cost/walk: A diffusion model makes an image by walking back from pure noise. At every step, its network reads every number of the picture, and guesses the noise in it.
cost/px: A five twelve by five twelve color image has three numbers per pixel, for red, green and blue: seven hundred and eighty six thousand, four hundred and thirty two in all. The network goes through every one of them again, at each of fifty steps.
cost/patch: Look closely at one small patch of sky, eight pixels by eight. That is a hundred and ninety two numbers, and they nearly all repeat one another.
cost/rombach: In 2021, Robin Rombach and colleagues made the point: most of an image's numbers carry detail the eye barely notices. Yet a diffusion model on pixels works through every one of them, at every step.
squeeze/enc: Their fix was to squeeze the image first, with an autoencoder, and run the diffusion on the squeezed version instead.
squeeze/grid: This encoder keeps the picture's layout. Out comes a small grid, and each spot of it sits over one patch of eight by eight pixels, described in just four numbers.
squeeze/z: That grid is the autoencoder's code, z. For a five twelve by five twelve image, it is sixty four by sixty four spots: the sizes Stable Diffusion used, in 2022.
squeeze/name: Here the code is called the latent, from the Latin for lying hidden: nobody looks at these numbers as a picture. Only the decoder turns them back into pixels.
squeeze/spots: Each side is eight times shorter, so the grid has eight times eight: sixty four times fewer spots than the image has pixels.
squeeze/count: But each spot holds four numbers, where a pixel holds three. That makes sixteen thousand, three hundred and eighty four numbers in all.
squeeze/ratio: Sixty four times fewer spots, with four numbers for every three: sixty four times three, over four, is forty eight. Forty eight times fewer numbers, at every step.
train/ae: So two networks are trained, one after the other. First the autoencoder, on images alone, as before: encode, decode, and match the input.
train/frozen: Then it is frozen: its weights never change again. That way, a latent keeps the same meaning while the second network learns from it.
train/dn: The second network is the denoiser. Each training image is encoded, and its latent, z, takes the place of the clean image.
train/zt: Blend z with noise to a random step t, exactly as with pixels, and you get z t: a noised latent.
train/loss: The denoiser learns to find that noise, with the same squared error as before. It never sees a pixel: its guess, epsilon hat, has the latent's shape.
make/start: To make a new image, start from pure noise in the latent's shape, sixty four by sixty four by four. There is no image to encode, so the encoder does not run at all.
make/loop: Then walk back, step after step. Each step runs the denoiser on just sixteen thousand, three hundred and eighty four numbers: fifty steps, fifty calls.
make/decode: Only at the very end does the decoder run, once, turning the finished latent into a five twelve by five twelve image.
